## Key takeaways


- **Use video primarily for recurring messages** where a reusable script and video format can save production time.
- **Keep important reference information in writing** when employees need to search, quote, or check exact wording later.
- **Use a real person for sensitive messages** where accountability, authenticity, or personal presence matters.
- **Treat the script as the source of truth** for approvals, updates, translations, and new video versions.
- **Start with one recurring communication format** and test production efficiency and employee outcomes before scaling.


Internal communications videos can make company updates easier to understand, more engaging, and more consistent across teams and locations. They work particularly well for recurring messages such as all-hands recaps, policy updates, onboarding modules, and multilingual announcements.


AI has also changed the economics of producing them. Instead of organizing a shoot every time something changes, teams can create or update a video directly from an approved script.[Text-to-video technology](https://www.d-id.com/blog/text-to-video-ai-revolutionizing-how-enterprises-communicate/) makes video a realistic option for messages that previously would have been sent as an email, document, or presentation.


That makes production easier. But it also raises a more important question:


**Which internal messages actually deserve a video?**


This guide will help you answer that question, choose the right use cases, build a repeatable workflow, and test whether AI video improves your internal communications.


## When should internal communications use video?


Video is not automatically better than an email, intranet post, meeting, or document.


The format should match what employees need to do with the information.


**Question** **Video is a good fit when** **Choose another format when**


**Does it repeat?** You send a similar message regularly It is a one-off update


**Do people need to reference it?** Employees mainly need to understand and act Employees need to search or quote exact wording


**Does a presenter help?** A face makes the message easier to follow A real leader needs to personally deliver the message


**Does it need localization?** The same message goes to several locations or languages It only affects one small group


**Is the message complex?** Explanation, examples, or visuals make it easier to understand A short email or Slack message would communicate it faster


The pressure to communicate more effectively is real. Gallup’s[State of the Global Workplace](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/349484/state-of-the-global-workplace.aspx) put global employee engagement at 20% in 2025, its lowest level since 2020. Gallagher’s State of the Sector research also found that 83% of communications and HR professionals see information overload as a growing issue for employees.


Neither statistic proves that video is the answer. But they do show why teams are looking for communication formats that can make important messages easier to absorb.


In the past, video was often ruled out because producing it required filming, editing, and external resources. AI video removes much of that overhead, allowing teams to choose the format based more on the communication goal itself.


## 5 practical use cases for internal communications videos


Some internal messages benefit much more from this workflow than others.


Here are five strong starting points.


### 1. All-hands recaps


A full recording of an all-hands meeting may be an hour long. Employees who missed the meeting rarely need every minute of it.


A short recap can focus on the decisions and actions that matter.


**Example:** Turn a 60-minute company meeting into a three-minute recap covering new priorities, key decisions, deadlines, and next steps.


AI video works particularly well here because the communication format repeats. Teams can reuse the same structure after every all-hands.


One important limitation remains: build the recap from what was actually decided, not only from the meeting agenda.


### 2. Policy and compliance updates


Policy changes are often communicated through PDFs or long emails. Employees may open them without clearly understanding what has changed or what they need to do.


A short video can provide the practical summary.


**Example:** Explain a new travel-expense policy in 90 seconds: what changed, who it affects, when the new rules start, and where employees can find the full policy.


When another paragraph changes later, the team can update the approved script and render a new version instead of producing another video from scratch.


The written policy should still remain the source for exact legal or contractual wording.


### 3. Executive messages


AI video can help when leadership needs to communicate frequently without organizing a new shoot every time.


**Example:** Create a regular monthly business update covering performance, priorities, and upcoming initiatives using an approved executive avatar.


This works best for routine communication.


For highly sensitive topics, however, a real executive should usually remain on camera. Layoffs, serious incidents, investigations, and apologies are situations where employees are also judging whether the leader was willing to personally show up.


### 4. Employee onboarding


Onboarding contains a large amount of information that organizations repeat for every new employee.


That makes it a natural candidate for reusable video.


**Example:** Create a short security onboarding module explaining password requirements, phishing risks, reporting procedures, and where employees can get help.


The script can then be updated whenever a policy changes without organizing another training session or video shoot.


For inspiration on how different training formats can be structured, these[e-learning video examples](https://www.d-id.com/blog/best-elearning-video-examples/) show several approaches to pacing, presentation, and content.


The main risk is neglecting maintenance. Assign clear ownership so somebody is responsible for keeping the scripts current.


### 5. Multi-location and multilingual communication


The production advantage becomes particularly clear when one message needs to reach employees across countries.


Traditionally, organizations might choose between subtitles, separate productions, or communicating primarily in one language.


With AI video, teams can work from one approved source script and produce localized versions.


For example, D-ID’s Creative Reality Studio supports avatar-led video in more than 120 languages. Its video translation capabilities can also translate finished videos into up to 29 languages while cloning the original speaker’s voice and adapting lip movements.


For policy, compliance, or safety communication, however, machine-translated wording should still be reviewed by someone who understands the language and context.


## Build the workflow around the script


When traditional video requires a shoot, the final footage becomes the central asset.


With AI-generated video, the **script can become the source of truth** .


Legal can review it. Leadership can approve it. Translators can localize it. And when something changes, the team edits the text before generating the next version.


That can make internal video fit much more naturally into existing approval processes.


[Diplomat Group](https://www.d-id.com/resources/case-study/diplomat-group-uses-d-id-to-transform-training/) , an FMCG distributor with more than 2,500 employees across Israel, Georgia, Cyprus, South Africa, and New Zealand, uses D-ID’s Creative Reality Studio as part of its training and communication workflow. Its global L&D team produces video with the platform and PowerPoint integration, while other departments can submit production requests to the team.


The lesson is not simply to adopt an AI video platform. It is to establish a repeatable workflow around it.


### Create a reusable script template


For recurring internal updates, every script should answer five questions:


1. **What changed?**
2. **Who does it affect?**
3. **What do those employees need to do?**
4. **By when?**
5. **Where can they ask questions?**


If AI-generated presenters are used, the template can also include a standard disclosure line so teams do not have to solve the same compliance question for every video.


### Keep a script library


Store the approved scripts alongside the finished videos.


When a policy or process changes next quarter, the script is usually the asset you need to update first.


### Re-render instead of restarting production


A changed sentence should require editing the source text, not planning another shoot.


That is one of the main operational advantages of script-based video production.


### Measure what employees actually do


Views and completion rates tell you whether people encountered the content.


They do not necessarily tell you whether the communication worked.


Gallagher’s State of the Sector research found that 70% of communications teams primarily measure output metrics such as page views, while only 16% measure outcomes such as employee sentiment.


For each video, decide what employee behavior should change.


For example:


- policy acknowledgements
- completed onboarding steps
- fewer support questions
- registration for an internal initiative
- completion of required training
- correct use of a new process


Choose this metric before publishing the video so you have a meaningful baseline.


Interactive formats can add another layer of insight. With[D-ID Agentic Videos](https://www.d-id.com/agentic-videos/) , employees can ask questions by voice or chat during playback and receive answers grounded in the video’s script. Those questions can also reveal where employees still need clarification, providing a more actionable signal than completion rate alone.


## When should you keep a real person on camera?


AI presenters can make recurring communication much easier to produce. That does not mean every leadership message should use one.


A simple rule helps:


**Keep a real person on camera when showing up is part of the message.**


That includes communication around:


- layoffs or restructuring
- serious workplace or safety incidents
- investigations
- apologies
- highly personal leadership messages
- recognition after a particularly difficult period


In these situations, employees are responding not only to the information but also to the person delivering it.


For less sensitive communication, realistic AI presenters can offer more flexibility. D-ID’s[V4 Expressive Avatars](https://www.d-id.com/introducing-v4-expressive-avatars/) , for example, are based on multi-sentiment recordings of real actors and allow the same presenter to deliver messages with different sentiments and styles.


There is another situation where video may not be the right format at all.


If employees need to repeatedly search, quote, or compare exact information, keep the authoritative version in a document. A video can summarize or explain the information, but it should point employees back to the source.


The same principle applies more broadly when[building trust in AI video](https://www.d-id.com/blog/building-trust-authentic-ai-video-narrative/) : be transparent about what is synthetic and keep genuinely human moments human.


## Using AI presenters in the EU: what internal communications teams should know


Organizations operating in the EU also need to consider the transparency requirements of the EU AI Act.


Since August 2, 2026, deployers of AI systems have disclosure obligations for relevant artificially generated or manipulated content.


For an internal communications team, the practical rule is straightforward:


**If employees are watching a realistic AI-generated presenter that could be taken for a real person, clearly disclose that the content is AI-generated.**


There are two separate responsibilities.


**The platform’s responsibility:** Providers have obligations around technically marking AI-generated outputs.


**Your responsibility:** The organization publishing the content must provide the required disclosure to the audience.


The European Commission’s[guidance on Article 50 transparency obligations](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/transparency-obligations-under-article-50-ai-act) makes clear that a machine-readable marker alone does not replace the deployer’s disclosure obligation.


For recurring internal videos, the simplest operational approach is to create an approved disclosure once and include it in the video or template by default.


D-ID-generated videos also carry a watermark by default, while personal avatars and cloned voices require documented consent.


For complex or sensitive cases, organizations should involve their legal teams rather than treating a standard template as legal advice.


## A 30-day pilot plan for internal communications videos


You do not need to redesign your entire communication strategy to find out whether AI video works for your organization.


Start with one format you already publish regularly.


### Week 1: Choose the use case and create the template


Pick one recurring communication format, such as a monthly update, policy announcement, or onboarding module.


Create the reusable script structure and agree on the approval process.


**Measure:** Your current production time and an existing communication metric such as attendance, open rate, acknowledgement rate, or completion.


### Week 2: Compare both formats


Create the same message using your current process and an avatar-led video.


Track the full effort, including:


- writing
- approvals
- production
- revisions
- publishing


**Measure:** Total production hours for each version.


### Week 3: Test an update


Make a deliberate change to the message after publication and update the video.


This tests one of the biggest potential advantages of script-based video: how quickly teams can respond when information changes.


**Measure:** Time from the edit request to the updated published video.


### Week 4: Test localization


Take the final version and create it in your two most important additional languages.


Have the localized scripts reviewed where accuracy matters.


**Measure:** Production effort by language and employee performance by location.


## How to decide whether the pilot worked


At the end of the month, ask three questions.


### 1. Did production become easier?


Compare the total production and review time with your existing process.


### 2. Did communication improve?


Look at the employee behavior you selected before the pilot, not only video views.


### 3. Did updating or localizing become easier?


Consider how quickly the team could make changes or create additional language versions.


If the workflow improved at least two of these areas, test it with a second recurring communication format.


If it did not, identify where the friction occurred before rolling the process out further.


The problem may not be the video technology itself. The approval process, writing quality, or choice of use case may need work first.

## FAQ


### How much do internal communications videos cost with AI?


AI changes the cost structure rather than simply making every video cheaper. Instead of paying for a new shoot and edit whenever information changes, organizations typically pay for platform access and rendering. Script writing, review, approval, and localization time should still be included when calculating the real production cost.


### How long should an internal communications video be?


There is no universal length that works for every internal communication. Start with the action employees need to take and include only the information required to support that action. If one video covers several unrelated decisions or topics, consider splitting it into separate videos.


### Do we need consent to create an AI version of an executive?


Yes. Platforms offering personal avatars or voice cloning generally require documented consent, including D-ID. Organizations should also agree on how that person’s digital likeness may be used. A standing policy covering permitted message types is safer than asking for approval separately for every video.


### Do we have to tell employees that a video was made with AI?


In the EU, transparency requirements under Article 50 of the EU AI Act apply to relevant AI-generated or manipulated content, including professional and business use. Organizations should clearly disclose realistic AI-generated presenters when required. Requirements outside the EU vary by jurisdiction.


## Start with one message you already send


The best first AI video is probably not a completely new communication format.


Choose something your team already produces regularly.


Turn that message into a reusable script. Create the video. Measure how long it takes. Change something and update it. Then test another language or audience.


Within a few iterations, you should know whether AI video solves a real communication problem or simply gives you another content format to manage.
